name: Common Buckwheat
summary: A fast-growing annual used as a short-window cover crop. University of Minnesota Extension reports quick establishment, weed suppression and flowers that support beneficial insects; its regional planting windows should not be generalized to every climate.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Fagopyrum esculentum. This profile represents common buckwheat, not a named grain or cover-crop variety.

growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes buckwheat as quick to establish and useful for weed suppression. Its crop-selection guidance is regional and does not establish indoor or hydroponic performance.

cultivation.short: Useful in a warm-season cover-crop window
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension lists June 10–August 15 as a Minnesota planting window and gives field seeding-rate guidance. Treat these as regional cover-crop references, not a local calendar or container rate.

management.short: Terminate around flowering to avoid reseeding
management.guidance: UMN Extension warns buckwheat can set seed quickly and advises termination at flowering to prevent reseeding. It can attract pollinators and beneficial insects if allowed to flower before termination.

propagation.short: Sowing is documented; home seedling protocol incomplete
propagation.guidance: Extension sources document planting windows and field seeding rates, but do not establish a complete home-garden sowing depth, germination temperature or seedling-stage protocol. Those details remain unresolved.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Cover-crop field guidance does not establish hydroponic suitability.

spacing.reason: Field seeding rates are not hydroponic pod spacing.

name: Crimson Clover
summary: An annual legume cover crop used for nitrogen contribution and soil cover. University of Minnesota guidance describes regional use and cautions that a pure stand may become weedy; it is not a hydroponic crop profile.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Trifolium incarnatum in Fabaceae. No named cultivar or seed product is represented.

growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes crimson clover as a legume used in cover-crop mixes and identifies its nitrogen contribution. The evidence is for agricultural/vegetable cover-crop use in Minnesota.

cultivation.short: Planting dates and rate depend on region and mix
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension recommends planting clover before grasses in a mix so the grass does not overtake it. Its planting recommendations and field rates are Minnesota references, not a universal garden schedule.

management.short: Mixing can support weed suppression; monitor reseeding
management.guidance: UMN Extension notes nitrogen fixation and some weed suppression in mixtures, and cautions crimson clover may become weedy when grown alone. It may support beneficial insects if allowed to flower before termination.

propagation.short: Seeded cover crop; detailed home protocol unresolved
propagation.guidance: The selected sources establish seeding as the cover-crop route and provide regional planting context, but do not document a complete home seed-starting protocol, depth or germination conditions.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Cover-crop and field-legume evidence does not establish hydroponic suitability.

name: White Clover
summary: A perennial legume used in groundcover and cover-crop mixes. Extension guidance supports nitrogen contribution and soil-cover functions; this species-level record does not claim a lawn cultivar or edible use.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Trifolium repens. This record is the species and not a named lawn or microclover selection.

growth.guidance: UMN Extension lists white clover among legume cover crops and reports soil-cover and nitrogen-source functions. These are cover-crop program characteristics, not guarantees for every garden site.

cultivation.short: Use as part of a planned cover-crop mix
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension compares white clover's cover-crop functions and discusses mixtures in vegetable production. Local persistence and competition depend on climate and management; no universal planting rate is assigned here.

management.short: Plan termination and prevent unwanted persistence
management.guidance: As a perennial groundcover, white clover may persist beyond a short cover-crop window. The selected Minnesota guides evaluate it as a field cover crop; a small-garden termination procedure is not established here.

propagation.short: Seeded cover crop; establishment details need validation
propagation.guidance: The Extension cover-crop guide supports use of white clover as a seeded cover crop but does not provide a complete home-garden germination protocol in the selected material. Depth and seedling-care details remain unresolved.

name: Cereal Rye
summary: A cool-season cereal widely used as an overwintering cover crop. University of Minnesota Extension describes reliable establishment and spring growth in Minnesota; management must account for termination before the next crop.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Secale cereale as a cultivated cereal species. This entry represents cereal rye, not annual ryegrass (Lolium) or a named grain cultivar.

growth.short: Cool-season cereal used for winter soil cover
growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes cereal rye as a common Minnesota cover crop that germinates at cool temperatures, establishes reliably and overwinters in the region. Performance depends on climate and planting window.

cultivation.short: Field timing is regional and rotation-dependent
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension lists regional planting windows and field-scale seeding rates. Its Minnesota dates should not be copied as a universal home-garden calendar or a container sowing rate.

management.short: Plan spring termination before the next crop
management.guidance: UMN Extension explains that overwintering rye generally needs termination before the following cash crop; later growth can make control more difficult and can compete for water. This is cover-crop management, not a food harvest recommendation.

propagation.guidance: UMN sources document drilling and field establishment, but do not establish a complete small-garden seedling protocol for this identity. Field rates and row geometry should not be presented as indoor pod guidance.

name: Oats
summary: A cool-season cereal used for grain, forage and short-window cover cropping. Minnesota Extension describes rapid establishment and winter-killed cover-crop use in its regional system; this is not a specific oat cultivar profile.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Avena sativa. No grain cultivar, forage selection or seed product is specified in this entry.

growth.guidance: Kew identifies Avena sativa as an annual cultivated species. UMN Extension includes oats among cover crops that can establish quickly and provide weed suppression and organic matter in its regional crop context.

cultivation.short: Short-window cover crop in regional rotations
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension gives Minnesota planting windows and field seeding rates for oats. These production figures are not converted into small-container or hydroponic spacing.

management.short: Often winter-killed in Minnesota cover-crop use
management.guidance: UMN Extension describes spring small grains such as oats as crops that typically do not overwinter in its Minnesota context. Winter survival varies with species, cultivar and conditions; this is not a universal guarantee.

propagation.short: Sowing is documented; home protocol remains incomplete
propagation.guidance: UMN Extension supports seed sowing in field cover-crop rotations, but the selected source set does not give a complete home-garden sowing and seedling protocol for this crop identity.

name: Alpine Strawberry
summary: A day-neutral strawberry species producing small fruits and useful for containers or perennial beds. University of Minnesota Extension distinguishes it from a cultivar: it is a separate species/type and may be grown from seed.

identity.short: Accepted species, distinct from garden strawberry cultivars
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Fragaria vesca. UMN Extension identifies alpine/woodland strawberry as a distinct species/type, not a named cultivar of Monterey strawberry; the entry does not assign a selection.

growth.guidance: UMN describes alpine strawberry as day-neutral, compact and able to grow in partial shade. It reports that this type does not produce runners, unlike many garden strawberry types; the guidance is Minnesota home-garden context.

cultivation.short: Suitable for beds, walkways or containers in its regional guide
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension says woodland strawberries tolerate shadier sites and can be planted in perennial beds, walkways or containers. This is soil/container guidance and does not establish hydroponic compatibility.

harvest.short: Small, sweet berries; yield differs from large-fruited types
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension describes small, sweet fruit and gives an approximate species-type yield of two to three berries per plant per week. This should not be generalized to other strawberry species or cultivars.

propagation.short: Seed-grown plants are represented; germination protocol not established
propagation.guidance: UMN notes that alpine strawberry plants are commonly grown from seed, but the selected source does not supply a complete sowing depth, temperature or germination protocol. Keep those details unresolved.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Container and garden-bed guidance does not establish hydroponic performance.

evidence.note: The species-type is described as small and runner-free, remaining in a compact plant form.

height.reason: No numeric species-level mature height is provided.

spread.reason: The source describes runner-free compact growth but no numeric footprint.

spacing.reason: Garden bed guidance is not indoor pod spacing.

light.reason: Outdoor partial shade is not an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Black Chokeberry
summary: A hardy deciduous shrub with edible but strongly astringent fruit, usually processed rather than eaten fresh. The species has landscape, wildlife and fruit uses; no named cultivar is assigned.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Aronia melanocarpa and records the common name black chokeberry. This is not chokecherry (Prunus virginiana), and no cultivar such as ‘Viking’ or ‘Autumn Magic’ is assigned.

growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes a deciduous shrub about 3–8 ft tall and 2–6 ft wide in its Minnesota landscape profile. It can sucker and form dense plantings; those regional dimensions are not a container-size promise.

cultivation.guidance: UMN reports full sun, tolerance of partial shade and broad soil/moisture tolerance, including wet soils, in Minnesota. These landscape conditions do not establish indoor or hydroponic suitability.

harvest.guidance: UMN describes dark fruit used in jams, juice, wine and baking, and notes it is too astringent for most people to eat raw. The source does not establish a home harvest calendar for an unnamed selection.

problems.short: Suckering and browsing are useful management signals
problems.guidance: UMN reports stronger suckering in cultivated landscapes and browsing by deer and rabbits; it lists no serious pest or stress problem in its regional profile. Absence from that list is not a guarantee of pest-free growth.

propagation.short: Home propagation route not established in selected sources
propagation.guidance: The selected Extension profile describes the plant but does not establish a seed, cutting or division protocol. Do not infer propagation from fruit containing seeds.

name: Honeyberry
summary: A cold-hardy blue-fruited honeysuckle crop also called haskap. Fruit production depends on compatible cultivars for cross-pollination; this species record does not name a cultivar or imply that one plant will fruit reliably.

identity.short: Accepted species; cultivar and subspecies unspecified
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Lonicera caerulea. The common names honeyberry and haskap are used for the cultivated fruit crop, but no subspecies or named cultivar is assigned here.

growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes honeyberry as a cold-climate fruit crop and lists the species as a shrub. Regional hardiness and fruit behavior vary with the cultivar and site.

cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension states that honeyberries need two compatible varieties. Its Minnesota table and crop guidance are regional and do not establish performance in indoor systems or all climates.

harvest.short: Early-season blue fruit; ripeness varies by variety
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension describes honeyberry harvest as early-season and reports variation in harvest timing and fruit traits among varieties. No cultivar-specific harvest window is assigned to this unnamed species-level record.

problems.short: Birds and powdery mildew may affect crops
problems.guidance: UMN's edible fruit table notes birds and powdery mildew as possible honeyberry problems. This does not imply that every plant will be affected.

propagation.short: Cultivar-preserving propagation route not established here
propagation.guidance: The selected sources do not give a home seed or vegetative propagation protocol. Seedling identity would not establish a named fruit cultivar; propagation details remain unresolved.

name: Lingonberry
summary: A low-growing, evergreen berry species associated with acidic soils and cold climates. University of Minnesota Extension provides regional landscape guidance; cultivar-specific performance and a home propagation protocol remain unresolved.

identity.short: Accepted species; common name cowberry is also used
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Vaccinium vitis-idaea and records cowberry among its English common names. The identity is not American cranberry (Vaccinium macrocarpon), already represented separately.

growth.guidance: Kew describes the accepted species as a subshrub. UMN Extension includes lingonberry as a low-growing edible landscape plant in its Minnesota comparison table; no specific cultivar is assigned.

cultivation.short: Acidic soil is a defining regional requirement
cultivation.guidance: UMN's table lists lingonberry for Minnesota zones 2–7 and a soil pH range of 4.0–5.5. This is regional soil-grown guidance and should not be transferred to other Vaccinium species or hydroponic solutions.

harvest.short: Edible fruit; selection and harvest details unresolved
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension includes lingonberry among edible fruit crops but the selected table does not provide a harvest calendar or cultivar-specific fruit-use protocol. Those details remain open.

propagation.guidance: The selected Extension source does not specify a seed-starting, cutting or division protocol for lingonberry. Keep propagation unresolved rather than inferring it from the genus.

name: Saskatoon Serviceberry
summary: A North American serviceberry species grown for edible blue-purple fruit and ornamental value. Species-specific taxonomy is resolved, while some landscape guidance applies to Amelanchier serviceberries as a group and is labeled accordingly.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Amelanchier alnifolia. UMN distinguishes Saskatoon serviceberry from other Amelanchier species and notes its fruit quality; common name serviceberry alone can refer to multiple species.

growth.short: Shrub or small tree; dimensions remain genus-scoped
growth.guidance: UMN Extension describes serviceberries collectively as shrubs or small trees and gives a wide size range across species and cultivars. Those dimensions are not assigned to A. alnifolia in this profile.

cultivation.short: Fruit-focused site guidance is general to serviceberries
cultivation.guidance: UMN says serviceberries grown for fruit produce best in full sun and prefer well-drained, lightly moist soils. The source covers several Amelanchier species; apply this as genus-level guidance, not a cultivar-specific guarantee.

harvest.short: Edible purple fruit used fresh or in preserves
harvest.guidance: UMN describes serviceberry fruit as edible fresh or for jams, jellies and pies, and identifies Saskatoon as producing the best-quality fruit among the listed Minnesota species. This is regional group guidance, not a named cultivar claim.

propagation.short: Home propagation method not established in selected sources
propagation.guidance: The selected Kew and UMN sources resolve identity and landscape use but do not document a complete home seed, cutting or layering protocol for this species. Propagation remains unresolved.
